Concise Clinical Note

Consult Summary:
- 37-year-old male with 3-day history of acute diarrhea (4–5 watery/loose stools daily), mild abdominal pain, single episode of vomiting; no blood or mucus.

History:
- Presenting complaint: Diarrhea ×3 days, 4–5 times/day, watery/loose; associated mild abdominal pain, one episode of vomiting, possible low-grade fever (“maybe a little bit”), decreased appetite but able to maintain oral fluids.
- Pertinent negatives: No blood or mucus in stool, no recent travel, no concerning food intake, no significant dehydration symptoms reported.
- Past medical history: Asthma.
- Medications: “Lexapro” inhaler (dose/route/frequency not documented); no other regular or OTC medications currently taken.
- Allergies: None reported.
- Family history: Father with hypertension; father died of bowel cancer at age 62.
- Social / preventive history: Not discussed.

Examination:
- Vitals: Not documented.
- General: Clinician notes patient “looks like not dehydrated.”
- No further examination findings documented.

Impression:
- Likely acute viral or self-limiting infectious gastroenteritis causing diarrhea.

Plan:
- Hydration: Encourage liberal oral fluids; start oral rehydration solution (e.g., Dioralyte, OTC) to replace electrolytes.
- Diet: Follow “soft” bland diet (e.g., crackers, toast, mashed/boiled vegetables). Avoid dairy, meat, fish, eggs while diarrhea persists. Yogurt (probiotics) allowed.
- Step-wise re-introduction: After 48 hours without diarrhea, gradually reintroduce meat/eggs/fish.
- Red-flag advice: Seek care if diarrhea persists >1 week, stool frequency increases to ≥6–8/day, signs of dehydration, or blood/mucus in stool. Stool sample and possible antibiotics may then be required; consider hospital assessment for dehydration if severe.
- Follow-up: Re-contact service if red flags occur or no improvement.

Quality checks:

● Missing expected elements: Full medication reconciliation (including confirmation of “Lexapro” use/type), detailed drug dosing, complete allergy review (drug/food/latex), vitals, social history (smoking, alcohol), immunization status.  
● Internal conflicts: Patient states asthma inhaler called “Lexapro”; clinician unsure (conflict noted).  
● Transcript quality: Generally clear; occasional minor inaudible words not affecting clinical content.
